examples.title: From wavelengths to a rough distance
examples.problem: In a nearby galaxy the H$\alpha$ line, with rest wavelength $656.3$ nm, is observed at $660.9$ nm. Take $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc and $c = 2.998\times10^5$ km/s, and estimate the distance, assuming the shift is entirely due to the Hubble flow.
steps: Redshift from the measured wavelengths: $z = \lambda_{\rm obs}/\lambda_{\rm rest} - 1 = 660.9/656.3 - 1 \approx 0.00701$.
Because $z \ll 1$ the low-redshift law applies. The apparent velocity is $cz \approx 2.998\times10^5 \times 0.00701 \approx 2.10\times10^3$ km/s.
Invert the Hubble–Lemaître law: $d = cz/H_0 \approx 2.10\times10^3 / 70 \approx 30$ Mpc.
State the caveat. A peculiar velocity of 300 km/s would change $cz$ by about 14%, so this is a rough distance, and the result is conditional on the assumed $H_0$.

examples.title: A supernova distance from its magnitudes
examples.problem: A Type Ia supernova has absolute magnitude $M = -19.3$ and apparent magnitude $m = 15.7$. Find its luminosity distance and the redshift expected at low $z$ for $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc.
steps: Distance modulus: $\mu = m - M = 15.7 - (-19.3) = 35.0$.
Invert $\mu = 5\log_{10}(d_L/10\ \mathrm{pc})$: $d_L = 10^{(\mu+5)/5}\ \mathrm{pc} = 10^{8}$ pc $= 100$ Mpc.
At low redshift $d_L\approx d$, so $z \approx H_0 d/c = 70\times 100/(2.998\times10^5) \approx 0.023$.
The assumed $M$ is a calibration, not a measurement of this object. Changing $M$ by $0.1$ mag changes $d_L$ by about 5%.

practice.prompt: The hydrogen Lyman-$\alpha$ line has rest wavelength $121.567$ nm. In a quasar spectrum it is observed at $486.268$ nm. Find the redshift $z$.
hints: Use $1+z = \lambda_{\rm obs}/\lambda_{\rm emit}$.
The ratio $486.268/121.567$ is a simple integer.

practice.prompt: A galaxy has a measured redshift $cz = 4200$ km/s, entirely due to the Hubble flow. Take $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc. How far away is it?
hints: At low redshift the Hubble–Lemaître law reads $cz = H_0 d$.

practice.prompt: Find the Hubble time $1/H_0$ in Gyr for $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc. Use $1\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 3.0857\times10^{19}$ km and $1\ \mathrm{Gyr} = 3.156\times10^{16}$ s. Round to two decimal places.
practice.solution: $1/H_0 = 3.0857\times10^{19}/70\ \mathrm{s} = 4.408\times10^{17}$ s. Dividing by $3.156\times10^{16}$ s/Gyr gives $13.97$ Gyr.
hints: Convert Mpc to km first so that the units of $H_0$ become s$^{-1}$.
$H_0 = 70/(3.0857\times10^{19})\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$; invert it to get seconds, then divide by the number of seconds in a Gyr.

practice.prompt: Which of the following is a direct measurement rather than a model-dependent inference?
practice.solution: Only the wavelength is recorded by the instrument. Recession velocity, comoving distance and emission epoch all require a model that connects the redshift to distances and times.
hints: Ask which of these quantities would change if you changed the assumed cosmological model but kept the data.
choices: The wavelength of a spectral line in a galaxy's spectrum.
The recession velocity of the galaxy.
The comoving distance to the galaxy.
The age of the universe when the light was emitted.

practice.prompt: Compute the present photon number density of the CMB in cm$^{-3}$ using $n_\gamma = \frac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}\left(\frac{k_BT_0}{\hbar c}\right)^3$ with $T_0 = 2.7255$ K, $k_B = 1.3806\times10^{-23}$ J/K, $\hbar = 1.0546\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c = 2.9979\times10^{8}$ m/s and $\zeta(3) = 1.2021$. Give the answer to three significant figures.
practice.solution: $k_BT_0/(\hbar c) \approx 1190\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Its cube is $1.686\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, and multiplying by $0.2436$ gives $4.11\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}} \approx 411\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$.
hints: First compute $k_BT_0/(\hbar c)$ in m$^{-1}$; it is of order $10^3$.
Cube it, multiply by $2\zeta(3)/\pi^2 \approx 0.2436$, and convert m$^{-3}$ to cm$^{-3}$ by dividing by $10^6$.

quiz.prompt: A Type Ia supernova has absolute magnitude $M = -19.3$ and is observed at apparent magnitude $m = 24.7$. Find its luminosity distance in Mpc, to three significant figures.
hints: Compute the distance modulus $\mu = m - M$ first.
Invert $\mu = 5\log_{10}(d_L/10\ \mathrm{pc})$ for $d_L$ in parsecs, then convert to Mpc.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are consequences or tests of the cosmological principle (statistical homogeneity and isotropy on large scales)?
quiz.solution: The CMB isotropy, the observer-independence of the velocity law and the large-scale uniformity of galaxy counts all follow from or test the principle. Peculiar velocities and local structure exist and are compatible with it, and an expanding homogeneous universe has no centre.
hints: Homogeneity is about position, isotropy about direction; neither says that small-scale structure is absent.
choices: After the dipole is removed, the CMB temperature is the same in all directions to about one part in $10^5$.
An observer in any other galaxy would measure the same Hubble–Lemaître law.
The average number of galaxies in spheres several hundred Mpc across does not depend on where the sphere is centred.
Galaxies have no peculiar velocities.
The universe has a centre from which all galaxies recede.

mistakes: Treating $cz$ as a literal velocity at large $z$; the formula $v = cz$ is only the low-redshift limit of the Hubble–Lemaître law.
Using very nearby galaxies to determine $H_0$, where peculiar velocities are comparable to the Hubble flow.
Mixing $h^{-1}$ Mpc with Mpc, or quoting a distance without saying which $H_0$ it assumes.
Reporting an inferred quantity (a distance, an age) as if it were a direct measurement.
lessons.title: Cosmic observations
lessons.summary: Separate what cosmology measures from what it infers, and use redshift, the Hubble–Lemaître law, the distance modulus and the blackbody CMB quantitatively.
objectives: State the cosmological principle and list the observational pillars of the hot big bang picture.
Convert between line wavelengths, redshift and low-redshift distance using the Hubble–Lemaître law.
Turn magnitudes and the CMB temperature into distances and photon densities, stating the units and conventions you use.
lessons.reading: Perimeter PSI Online course collection, Cosmology module: the introductory notes on the expanding universe, the cosmological principle and the cosmic microwave background (look up the topics "Hubble law" and "CMB blackbody").
lessons.article:
Cosmology has one sky, one vantage point and no repeatable experiments, so the first skill is bookkeeping: which numbers did a telescope record, and which came out of a model?

### Conventions for this course

Unless stated otherwise: SI units (or km/s, Mpc and Gyr where customary); metric signature $(-,+,+,+)$; scale factor normalized to $a(t_0)=1$ today; $H_0 = 100\,h\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$; $1\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 3.0857\times10^{22}$ m; $c = 2.998\times10^{5}$ km/s.

The fiducial parameter values are approximate standard values from CMB-based fits to flat $\Lambda$CDM. Check them against current data before relying on them: $H_0\approx 67.4$ km/s/Mpc, $\Omega_m\approx 0.315$, $\Omega_\Lambda\approx 0.685$, $\Omega_b h^2\approx 0.0224$, $\Omega_c h^2\approx 0.120$, $T_0\approx 2.7255$ K, $n_s\approx 0.965$, $A_s\approx 2.1\times10^{-9}$. Local distance-ladder measurements give $H_0\approx 73$; this disagreement, the Hubble tension, returns in week 10. Every numerical problem here states the values it uses.

### Measured versus inferred

| Measured | Inferred through a model |
|---|---|
| wavelengths of spectral lines, hence the redshift $z$ | recession velocity, distance, look-back time |
| flux $F$ or apparent magnitude $m$ | luminosity $L$, absolute magnitude $M$ |
| angular positions and sizes | physical or comoving sizes |
| the microwave temperature on the sky | densities, $H_0$, spatial curvature |

A sentence such as "the galaxy is 30 Mpc away" always hides a model. The redshift is the cleanest number you will ever have.

### The pillars of the hot big bang picture

- **Expansion.** Spectral lines of distant galaxies are shifted to longer wavelengths. Define $1+z = \lambda_{\rm obs}/\lambda_{\rm emit}$.
- **A relic blackbody.** The sky glows at $T_0\approx 2.7255$ K with a spectrum that is a blackbody to high precision. Its energy density and number density are
$$u_\gamma=\frac{\pi^2}{15}\frac{(k_BT)^4}{(\hbar c)^3},\qquad n_\gamma=\frac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}\left(\frac{k_BT}{\hbar c}\right)^3\approx 411\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}.$$
- **Light elements.** Helium near 25% of the baryonic mass and deuterium near $2.5\times10^{-5}$ of hydrogen by number (week 6).
- **Structure.** Galaxies, clusters and a cosmic web whose statistics match nearly scale-invariant initial fluctuations (weeks 8 and 11).

### The cosmological principle

On scales above roughly 100 Mpc the universe appears statistically **homogeneous** (the same at every position) and **isotropic** (the same in every direction). Isotropy about every point implies homogeneity, and for an expanding universe it also forces the velocity law $v\propto d$ for every observer. The principle is an assumption that observations test. The CMB temperature is the same in all directions to about $10^{-5}$ once the dipole caused by our own motion (about 3.4 mK, a speed near 370 km/s) is removed.

### The Hubble–Lemaître law

For $z\ll 1$,
$$cz \simeq H_0\, d .$$
Two practical limits. First, galaxies also move relative to the Hubble flow with peculiar velocities of a few hundred km/s, so along the line of sight $cz = H_0 d + v_{\rm pec}$, and nearby galaxies give poor distances. Second, this is a low-redshift approximation: for $z\gtrsim 0.1$ you need the distance definitions of week 2. Two scales follow: the Hubble time $1/H_0 = 9.778\,h^{-1}$ Gyr and the Hubble distance $c/H_0 = 2998\,h^{-1}$ Mpc.

### Candles, rulers and magnitudes

A source of known luminosity $L$ with measured flux $F$ defines the luminosity distance through $F = L/(4\pi d_L^2)$. In astronomical magnitudes the **distance modulus** is
$$\mu \equiv m - M = 5\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{d_L}{10\ \mathrm{pc}}\right).$$
Type Ia supernovae are standardizable candles, the baryon acoustic oscillation scale (about 150 Mpc comoving) is a standard ruler, and merging compact binaries are standard sirens. Each is only as good as its calibration.

### A dark night sky is data

In an infinite, static, eternal universe every line of sight would end on a stellar surface and the night sky would be as bright as a star. A finite age together with redshift removes the paradox, so even the darkness of the night sky is a cosmological observation.

examples.title: Distances in an Einstein–de Sitter universe
examples.problem: In a flat, matter-only universe (derived in week 3) $H(z) = H_0(1+z)^{3/2}$. With $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc and $c = 299792$ km/s, find $D_M$, $d_L$ and $d_A$ for a source at $z=3$.
steps: In a flat universe $D_M = \chi = (c/H_0)\int_0^z (1+z')^{-3/2}\,dz'$.
Luminosity distance: $d_L = (1+z)D_M = 4\times 4283 \approx 17{,}130$ Mpc.
Angular-diameter distance: $d_A = D_M/(1+z) = 4283/4 \approx 1071$ Mpc, and indeed $d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A = 16\times 1071$.

examples.title: Proper distance, angle and flux for one galaxy
examples.problem: A galaxy at $z=2$ has comoving distance $\chi = 6000$ Mpc in a flat universe. Find its proper distance now and at emission, its $d_A$ and $d_L$, and the angle subtended by a $30$ kpc structure.
steps: The scale factor at emission is $a_e = 1/(1+z) = 1/3$.
Proper distance now is $a_0\chi = 6000$ Mpc; at emission it was $a_e\chi = 2000$ Mpc.
Flat, so $D_M = 6000$ Mpc. Then $d_A = 6000/3 = 2000$ Mpc (equal to the proper distance at emission) and $d_L = 3\times 6000 = 18{,}000$ Mpc.
The angle is $\theta = \ell/d_A = 0.030/2000 = 1.5\times10^{-5}$ rad $\approx 3.1$ arcsec.

practice.prompt: A galaxy is observed at redshift $z = 1.5$. What was the scale factor when the light was emitted (with $a_0 = 1$)?
hints: Use $1+z = a_0/a_e$.

practice.prompt: A universe expands as $a(t) = (t/t_0)^p$ with constant $p>0$. Give the Hubble parameter $H(t)$ in terms of $p$ and $t$.
practice.solution: $\dot a/a = d\ln a/dt = p/t$. It does not depend on $t_0$.
hints: $H = \dot a/a$.
Differentiate $\ln a = p\ln(t/t_0)$ with respect to $t$.

practice.prompt: A supernova at $z=0.5$ lies at transverse comoving distance $D_M = 1900$ Mpc. What is its luminosity distance?

Take a flat universe with $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, $\Omega_m = 0.3$, $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7$ and no radiation, so $H(z) = H_0\sqrt{0.3(1+z)^3 + 0.7}$. Use $c = 299792$ km/s. Find the comoving distance to $z = 1$ in Mpc, to four significant figures.
practice.solution: The integral is about $0.7714$. Multiplying by $c/H_0 = 4282.7$ Mpc gives $\chi \approx 3304$ Mpc.
hints: $\chi = c\int_0^1 dz/H(z)$; factor out $c/H_0 \approx 4283$ Mpc.
Evaluate $\int_0^1 [0.3(1+z)^3 + 0.7]^{-1/2}dz$ numerically (Simpson's rule with four intervals is enough); it is close to $0.77$.

practice.prompt: Write a short conventions sheet for FLRW calculations. Define the scale factor (with its normalization), the redshift, the Hubble parameter, and the comoving, luminosity and angular-diameter distances. State the metric signature and units, give the relations among the distances, and say which observable each distance goes with.
practice.solution: Signature $(-,+,+,+)$; units: lengths in Mpc, $H$ in km/s/Mpc, $c$ in km/s. Scale factor $a(t)$ with $a(t_0)=1$; comoving coordinates are fixed for comoving observers. Redshift $1+z = \lambda_{\rm obs}/\lambda_{\rm emit} = a_0/a_e = 1/a_e$. Hubble parameter $H = \dot a/a$. Comoving distance $\chi = c\int_0^z dz'/H(z')$; transverse comoving distance $D_M = S_K(\chi)$ with $S_K = \sin(\sqrt{K}\chi)/\sqrt{K}$, $\chi$, or $\sinh(\sqrt{-K}\chi)/\sqrt{-K}$. Luminosity distance $d_L = (1+z)D_M$ goes with flux, $F = L/4\pi d_L^2$; angular-diameter distance $d_A = D_M/(1+z)$ goes with angular sizes, $\theta = \ell/d_A$; and $d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A$. Comoving rulers (BAO) subtend $\theta = r/D_M$. Redshift, flux and angle are measured; the distances are inferred in a model.
hints: Write the definitions first, then the relations among the distances, then decide which quantities a telescope actually records.
rubric: States $a(t_0)=1$, $1+z = a_0/a_e$ and $H = \dot a/a$ with units.
Gives $\chi = c\int dz/H$, $D_M = S_K(\chi)$, $d_L = (1+z)D_M$, $d_A = D_M/(1+z)$ and $d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A$.
States the signature and units, and pairs each distance with the observable that uses it.
Distinguishes measured quantities (redshift, flux, angle) from inferred ones (distances).

quiz.prompt: A closed universe has curvature radius $R = 10{,}000$ Mpc, that is $K = 1/R^2$. A source lies at comoving distance $\chi = 3000$ Mpc. Find the transverse comoving distance $D_M = S_K(\chi)$ in Mpc.
quiz.solution: $D_M = R\sin(\chi/R) = 10{,}000\times\sin(0.3) = 10{,}000\times 0.29552 \approx 2955$ Mpc, slightly less than the flat value $3000$ Mpc.
hints: For $K>0$, $S_K(\chi) = \sin(\sqrt{K}\chi)/\sqrt{K}$ with $\sqrt{K} = 1/R$.
$\chi/R = 0.3$ radians.

quiz.prompt: Select all correct statements about FLRW cosmology.
quiz.solution: Along a comoving worldline $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2$, so $d\tau = dt$. Recession faster than $c$ is not a relative velocity in a local inertial frame. For flat space $D_M = \chi$ and $d_L = (1+z)D_M$. Redshift is stretching by $a$, not a Doppler shift, and $d_A$ has a maximum (near $z\approx 1.6$ in the benchmark model, $z=1.25$ in Einstein–de Sitter).
hints: Check each statement against the metric: what does $ds^2$ reduce to along a comoving worldline, and along a light ray?
choices: Comoving observers have fixed $(\chi,\theta,\varphi)$, so their proper time equals cosmic time $t$.
A galaxy beyond the Hubble sphere has $H d_{\rm prop} > c$, and this does not violate special relativity.
In a flat universe the luminosity distance is $d_L = (1+z)\chi$.
The cosmological redshift is a relativistic Doppler shift from the relative velocity of the source at emission, valid at any $z$.
The angular-diameter distance increases monotonically with redshift.

mistakes: Using $d_L$ where an angle needs $d_A$ (or $D_M$ for a comoving ruler); the two differ by factors of $(1+z)^2$.
Treating $c/H$ as the horizon, or $z$ as a Doppler velocity at high redshift.
Forgetting the curvature function: for $K\neq 0$ the transverse distance is $S_K(\chi)$, not $\chi$.
Mixing proper and comoving lengths, for example comparing a comoving BAO scale with a proper size without the factor $a$.
lessons.title: FLRW geometry
lessons.summary: Write the FLRW metric, define the scale factor, redshift and the comoving, proper, luminosity and angular-diameter distances, and compute them in simple cases.
objectives: Write the FLRW line element with signature (-,+,+,+) and identify comoving observers and cosmic time.
Derive 1+z = a_0/a_e from null geodesics and use it with the Hubble parameter H = \dot a/a.
Compute comoving, luminosity and angular-diameter distances, including the curvature function S_K.

lessons.article:
Homogeneity and isotropy fix the geometry of space up to one number (the curvature) and one function of time (the scale factor). Picture a grid drawn on a balloon that is being inflated. The grid labels, the **comoving coordinates**, never change, but the physical distance between grid points grows in proportion to the balloon's radius. That radius is the **scale factor** $a(t)$.

### The metric

With signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and the normalization $a(t_0)=1$, the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) line element is
$$ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + a^2(t)\left[d\chi^2 + S_K^2(\chi)\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\, d\varphi^2\right)\right],$$
where $t$ is **cosmic time**, $\chi$ is the radial comoving coordinate (a length), and
$$S_K(\chi)=\begin{cases}\sin(\sqrt{K}\,\chi)/\sqrt{K}, & K>0\ \text{(closed)}\\[2pt] \chi, & K=0\ \text{(flat)}\\[2pt] \sinh(\sqrt{-K}\,\chi)/\sqrt{-K}, & K<0\ \text{(open)}.\end{cases}$$
The constant $K$ has units of length$^{-2}$ and is the curvature of space today. A **comoving observer** has fixed $(\chi,\theta,\varphi)$, so $d\tau = dt$ along its worldline: cosmic time is the proper time of observers at rest in the expansion.

### Redshift from the metric

Two successive wavecrests leave a comoving source at $t_e$ and $t_e+\delta t_e$ and arrive at $t_0$ and $t_0+\delta t_0$. A radial light ray has $c\,dt = -a\,d\chi$, so the comoving path is the same for both and $\delta t_e/a_e = \delta t_0/a_0$. Wavelengths scale like time intervals, so
$$1+z = \frac{\lambda_{\rm obs}}{\lambda_{\rm emit}} = \frac{a(t_0)}{a(t_e)} = \frac{1}{a_e}.$$
Cosmological redshift is the stretching of wavelengths with the scale factor, not a Doppler shift of a photon moving through space. The two agree to first order at low $z$.

### The Hubble parameter and the distances

Define $H \equiv \dot a/a$. For a source at redshift $z$:

- **Proper distance** between comoving points at time $t$: $d_{\rm prop} = a(t)\chi$, so $\dot d_{\rm prop} = H d_{\rm prop}$.
- **Comoving distance**: $\displaystyle \chi = c\int_{t_e}^{t_0}\frac{dt}{a} = c\int_0^z \frac{dz'}{H(z')}$.
- **Transverse comoving distance**: $D_M = S_K(\chi)$, equal to $\chi$ when flat.
- **Luminosity distance**, defined by $F = L/(4\pi d_L^2)$: $d_L = (1+z)D_M$.
- **Angular-diameter distance**, defined by $\theta = \ell/d_A$ for proper size $\ell$ at emission: $d_A = D_M/(1+z)$.

Together these give the distance-duality relation $d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A$. For a flat universe $d_A = a_e\chi$ is the proper distance at the moment of emission.

### Horizons and the Hubble sphere

The **particle horizon** $\chi_p = c\int_0^t dt'/a$ is the farthest comoving distance from which a signal could have reached us. The **Hubble sphere** $c/H$ is a different thing: galaxies beyond it have $H d_{\rm prop} > c$, but this is not a relative velocity in a local inertial frame, so special relativity is not violated. Light emitted from beyond the Hubble sphere can still reach us, because the Hubble sphere itself moves. What limits the observable region is the particle horizon (in the past) and the event horizon (in the future), not $c/H$.

### Practical cautions

Always name the distance. $d_A$ is not monotonic in $z$ (for the benchmark model it peaks near $z\approx 1.6$), $d_L$ is what supernova fluxes measure, and $D_M$ is what BAO and CMB angles use. Keep a short conventions sheet: signature, $a(t_0)=1$, the definition of each distance, and the units.

examples.title: The critical density today
examples.problem: Find $\rho_{c,0}$ for $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, using $G = 6.674\times10^{-11}$ m$^3$ kg$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ and $1\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 3.0857\times10^{22}$ m. Express it as a number of proton masses ($1.673\times10^{-27}$ kg) per cubic metre.
steps: Convert $H_0$ to SI: $H_0 = 70\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}\,/\,3.0857\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{m} = 2.269\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
Apply the definition: $\rho_{c,0} = 3H_0^2/(8\pi G) = 1.544\times10^{-35}/1.677\times10^{-9} = 9.20\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
Divide by the proton mass: $9.20\times10^{-27}/1.673\times10^{-27} \approx 5.5$ protons per cubic metre. The whole universe is a very good vacuum.

examples.title: The age of a matter-only universe
examples.problem: Solve the Friedmann equation for a flat universe containing only pressureless matter, and find its age in terms of $H_0$.
steps: With $K=\Lambda=0$ and $\rho = \rho_0 a^{-3}$, the Friedmann equation reads $\dot a^2/a^2 = H_0^2 a^{-3}$, using $\rho_0 = \rho_{c,0}$ for flatness.
Take the positive root: $\dot a = H_0 a^{-1/2}$. Separate variables: $a^{1/2}\,da = H_0\,dt$.
Integrate from the big bang ($a=0$ at $t=0$): $\tfrac23 a^{3/2} = H_0 t$, so $a(t) = \left(\tfrac32 H_0 t\right)^{2/3}$.

Set $a=1$: $t_0 = 2/(3H_0)$. For $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, $1/H_0 = 13.97$ Gyr so $t_0 = 9.3$ Gyr, younger than the oldest stars. A pure matter model is too young, one reason a cosmological constant is needed.

practice.prompt: Compute the critical density for $H_0 = 100$ km/s/Mpc ($h=1$) in kg/m$^3$. Use $G = 6.674\times10^{-11}$ m$^3$ kg$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ and $1\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 3.0857\times10^{22}$ m. Give the answer in scientific notation to four significant figures.
hints: Convert $H_0$ to s$^{-1}$ first: $10^5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ divided by the number of metres in a Mpc.
Use $\rho_c = 3H^2/(8\pi G)$.

practice.prompt: A flat universe contains only pressureless matter and has $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc. Find its age in Gyr, using $1\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 3.0857\times10^{19}$ km and $1\ \mathrm{Gyr} = 3.156\times10^{16}$ s. Give two decimal places.
hints: $t_0 = \int_0^1 da/(aH)$ and here $H = H_0 a^{-3/2}$.
The integral gives $t_0 = 2/(3H_0)$; the Hubble time $1/H_0$ is $13.97$ Gyr.

practice.prompt: A fluid with constant $w = p/(\rho c^2)$ obeys $\dot\rho + 3H(1+w)\rho = 0$. Give $\rho(a)/\rho_0$, where $\rho_0$ is the density at $a=1$.
hints: Use $\dot\rho = (d\rho/da)\,\dot a$ and $H = \dot a/a$ to turn the equation into one for $d\rho/da$.
You get $d\ln\rho = -3(1+w)\,d\ln a$; integrate from $a=1$.

practice.prompt: A flat universe has $\Omega_m = 0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7$ (radiation neglected), so $\dot a = H_0\, a\sqrt{0.3\,a^{-3} + 0.7}$. Find the present deceleration parameter $q_0 = -\ddot a\,a/\dot a^2$.
practice.solution: Let $f(a) = \dot a/H_0 = \sqrt{0.3/a + 0.7a^2}$. Then $f(1) = 1$ and $f'(1) = (-0.3 + 1.4)/2 = 0.55$, so $q_0 = -0.55$. This agrees with $\Omega_m/2 - \Omega_\Lambda = 0.15 - 0.7$.
hints: Write $\ddot a = (d\dot a/da)\,\dot a$.
At $a=1$ we have $\dot a = H_0$, so $q_0 = -(d\dot a/da)/H_0$ evaluated at $a=1$.

practice.prompt: In a flat universe with $\Omega_m = 0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7$ (radiation neglected), the expansion changed from decelerating to accelerating at some redshift $z_{\rm acc}$. Find it, to three decimal places.
hints: Set $\ddot a = 0$ in the acceleration equation, which gives $\rho_m = 2\rho_\Lambda$ for dust plus a cosmological constant.
$\rho_m \propto \Omega_m(1+z)^3$ while $\rho_\Lambda$ is constant, so $(1+z)^3 = 2\Omega_\Lambda/\Omega_m$.

quiz.prompt: For a flat universe with $\Omega_m = 0.315$, $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.685$ (radiation neglected) and $H_0 = 67.4$ km/s/Mpc, find the age in Gyr. Use $1\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 3.0857\times10^{19}$ km and $1\ \mathrm{Gyr} = 3.156\times10^{16}$ s. Give two decimal places.
quiz.solution: $1/H_0 = 14.51$ Gyr. The dimensionless integral equals $\frac{2}{3\sqrt{0.685}}\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{0.685/0.315} = 0.9510$, so $t_0 = 0.9510\times 14.51 = 13.80$ Gyr.
hints: Rewrite the integrand as $a^{1/2}/\sqrt{0.315 + 0.685\,a^3}$ to see that it is finite at $a=0$. The closed form $\frac{2}{3\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda}}\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda/\Omega_m}$ also works.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following, if it dominated a flat universe, would give accelerating expansion ($\ddot a>0$)?
quiz.solution: The condition is strictly $w<-1/3$. Dust and radiation decelerate. Curvature alone gives $a\propto t$, coasting with $\ddot a=0$, not acceleration.
hints: Acceleration needs $\rho c^2 + 3p<0$, that is $w<-1/3$.
choices: A cosmological constant ($w=-1$).
A fluid with $w = -2/3$.
Pressureless dust ($w=0$).
Radiation ($w=1/3$).
Spatial curvature alone (an empty open universe, effective $w=-1/3$).

mistakes: Mixing mass density and energy density: with $\rho$ a mass density the pressure enters as $p/c^2$.
Concluding that acceleration needs negative pressure alone: it needs $w<-1/3$, that is $\rho c^2 + 3p < 0$.
Using $a\propto t^{2/3}$ when radiation or $\Lambda$ matters, or forgetting that the exponent is $2/[3(1+w)]$ only for a single constant-$w$ fluid.
Forgetting to convert $H_0$ from km/s/Mpc to s$^{-1}$ before computing densities or ages.

lessons.summary: Use the Friedmann, acceleration and fluid equations to find how a flat universe with one component expands, and compute critical density, ages and the sign of acceleration.
objectives: Write the Friedmann, acceleration and continuity equations and say how they are related.
Use the equation-of-state parameter w to get ρ(a) and the expansion law a(t) for matter, radiation and a cosmological constant.

lessons.article:
Start with a Newtonian picture. Take a uniform ball of dust and look at a test particle at radius $R = a\,r$ on its surface. Energy per unit mass is conserved: $\tfrac12\dot R^2 - GM/R = \text{const}$. With $M = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3\rho$ this becomes $H^2 = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \text{const}/R^2$. General relativity keeps this structure, reinterprets the constant as spatial curvature, and adds pressure.

### The equations

Assume a perfect fluid with mass density $\rho$ (so the energy density is $\rho c^2$) and pressure $p$, and define $w \equiv p/(\rho c^2)$. Inserting the FLRW metric of week 2 (signature $(-,+,+,+)$, $a(t_0)=1$) into Einstein's equations gives
$$H^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{Kc^2}{a^2} + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3},\qquad \frac{\ddot a}{a} = -\frac{4\pi G}{3}\left(\rho + \frac{3p}{c^2}\right) + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3},$$
and the energy-conservation (fluid) equation
$$\dot\rho + 3H\left(\rho + \frac{p}{c^2}\right) = 0 .$$
Only two of the three are independent. It is often convenient to absorb the cosmological constant into the fluid as a component with $w=-1$ and $\rho_\Lambda = \Lambda c^2/(8\pi G)$.

### How densities dilute

For constant $w$, the fluid equation gives $d\rho/\rho = -3(1+w)\,da/a$, so
$$\rho \propto a^{-3(1+w)} .$$
Pressureless matter ($w=0$) dilutes as $a^{-3}$, radiation ($w=1/3$) as $a^{-4}$ (the extra factor is the redshift of each photon), and a cosmological constant ($w=-1$) does not dilute. The curvature term in the Friedmann equation scales as $a^{-2}$, so it mimics a fluid with $w=-1/3$.

### Critical density and density parameters

Define $\rho_c(t) \equiv 3H^2/(8\pi G)$ and $\Omega_i \equiv \rho_i/\rho_c$. Today
$$\rho_{c,0} = 1.878\times10^{-26}\,h^2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} = 2.775\times10^{11}\,h^2\ M_\odot\,\mathrm{Mpc^{-3}} .$$
Dividing the Friedmann equation by $H^2$ gives $\sum_i\Omega_i + \Omega_K = 1$ with $\Omega_K \equiv -Kc^2/(a_0H_0)^2$. The total $\Omega_{\rm tot} = \sum_i \Omega_i$ exceeds 1 for a closed universe ($K>0$) and is below 1 for an open one.

### Single-component flat universes

If one fluid dominates and $K=0$, then $H^2 \propto a^{-3(1+w)}$, so $\dot a \propto a^{-(1+3w)/2}$ and integrating gives
$$a \propto t^{2/[3(1+w)]}\quad (w\neq -1),\qquad a\propto e^{H_\Lambda t}\quad (w=-1).$$
Matter: $a\propto t^{2/3}$ with $H = 2/(3t)$. Radiation: $a \propto t^{1/2}$ with $H = 1/(2t)$. A cosmological constant: exponential growth with $H_\Lambda = \sqrt{\Lambda c^2/3}$. The age of a flat matter-only universe is $t_0 = 2/(3H_0)$.

### Acceleration

The acceleration equation shows that $\ddot a>0$ requires $\rho c^2 + 3p < 0$, that is $w<-1/3$ for a single fluid. Gravity is sourced by pressure as well as by energy density. The **deceleration parameter** is $q \equiv -\ddot a\, a/\dot a^2$; for a flat universe with matter and $\Lambda$,
$$q_0 = \frac{\Omega_m}{2} - \Omega_\Lambda .$$

### Several components

In general $H(a) = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r a^{-4} + \Omega_m a^{-3} + \Omega_K a^{-2} + \Omega_\Lambda}$, and the age follows by integrating $dt = da/(aH)$:
$$t(a) = \int_0^a \frac{da'}{a' H(a')} .$$
For flat matter plus $\Lambda$ the integral has a closed form, $t_0 = \dfrac{2}{3H_0\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda}}\sinh^{-1}\!\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda/\Omega_m}$, which is a quick check on a numerical code.

examples.title: The photon density parameter
examples.problem: Compute $\rho_\gamma$ and $\Omega_\gamma h^2$ for $T_0 = 2.7255$ K, using $a_{\rm rad} = 7.566\times10^{-16}$ J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-4}$, $c = 2.998\times10^{8}$ m/s and $\rho_{c,0} = 1.878\times10^{-26}\,h^2$ kg m$^{-3}$.
steps: Energy density: $u_\gamma = a_{\rm rad}T_0^4 = 7.566\times10^{-16}\times 55.18 = 4.175\times10^{-14}$ J m$^{-3}$.
Convert to mass density: $\rho_\gamma = u_\gamma/c^2 = 4.175\times10^{-14}/8.988\times10^{16} = 4.645\times10^{-31}$ kg m$^{-3}$.
Divide by the critical density: $\Omega_\gamma = 4.645\times10^{-31}/(1.878\times10^{-26}h^2)$, so $\Omega_\gamma h^2 = 2.47\times10^{-5}$.
For $h=0.674$ this is $\Omega_\gamma = 5.4\times10^{-5}$: the photons are a tiny fraction of the critical density today, but they were dominant in the early universe because they dilute as $a^{-4}$.

examples.title: Matter–radiation equality
examples.problem: Take $\Omega_m h^2 = 0.1424$, $\Omega_\gamma h^2 = 2.473\times10^{-5}$ and $N_{\rm eff} = 3.046$. Find $\Omega_r h^2$ and the redshift of matter–radiation equality.
steps: The neutrino factor is $0.2271\times 3.046 = 0.6918$, so the total radiation parameter is $\Omega_r h^2 = 2.473\times10^{-5}\times 1.6918 = 4.184\times10^{-5}$.
The $h^2$ factors cancel in the ratio: $1+z_{\rm eq} = \Omega_m/\Omega_r = 0.1424/(4.184\times10^{-5}) = 3403$.
Therefore $z_{\rm eq}\approx 3400$, well before recombination at $z\approx 1090$ (week 7).
Equality is set by physical densities $\Omega_m h^2$ and $\Omega_r h^2$ alone, so it is independent of $\Omega_\Lambda$ and of the Hubble constant taken separately.

practice.prompt: By what factor is the mean matter density larger at redshift $z=2$ than today?
hints: Matter dilutes as the volume grows: $\rho_m\propto a^{-3}$.

practice.prompt: The curvature term $-Kc^2/a^2$ in the Friedmann equation scales like $a^{-2}$. It therefore behaves like a fluid with which equation-of-state parameter?
Take $\Omega_m h^2 = 0.1424$ and $\Omega_r h^2 = 4.184\times10^{-5}$. What is the ratio of radiation energy density to matter density at recombination, $z = 1089$? Give three significant figures.
hints: Radiation dilutes as $(1+z)^4$ and matter as $(1+z)^3$, so the ratio grows as $(1+z)$.
At $z=0$ the ratio is $\Omega_r/\Omega_m$.

practice.prompt: For a flat universe with $\Omega_m = 0.315$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.685$, find the redshift at which the matter density equals the dark-energy density. Give three decimal places.
hints: The cosmological-constant density does not change; the matter density grows as $(1+z)^3$ into the past.

practice.prompt: Starting from the Friedmann equation for a flat universe containing only radiation, derive $a(t)$ up to a constant, then $H(t)$ and $\rho_r(t)$. Then use $\rho_r\propto T^4$ to find how the temperature depends on time.
practice.solution: Flat, radiation only: $H^2 = (8\pi G/3)\rho_r$ with $\rho_r = \rho_{r,0}a^{-4}$, so $\dot a^2 = H_0^2\Omega_r a^{-2}$ and $\dot a = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r}/a$. Separate: $a\,da = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r}\,dt$, so $a^2 = 2H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r}\,t$ and $a\propto t^{1/2}$. Then $H = \dot a/a = 1/(2t)$. From the Friedmann equation, $\rho_r = 3H^2/(8\pi G) = 3/(32\pi G t^2)$. Since $\rho_r\propto T^4$, $T\propto \rho_r^{1/4}\propto t^{-1/2}$, consistent with $T\propto 1/a$.
hints: Use $\rho_r\propto a^{-4}$ in the Friedmann equation, take the positive root for $\dot a$, and separate variables.
rubric: Separates variables correctly and integrates to $a\propto t^{1/2}$ with the boundary condition $a(0)=0$.
Obtains $H = 1/(2t)$ and $\rho_r = 3/(32\pi G t^2)$ from the Friedmann equation.
Concludes $T\propto t^{-1/2}$ using $\rho_r\propto T^4$ and checks consistency with $T\propto 1/a$.

quiz.prompt: In a flat universe with $\Omega_m = 0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7$ (radiation neglected), at what redshift does matter make up 90% of the total energy density? Give three decimal places.
hints: The matter fraction is $\Omega_m(1+z)^3/[\Omega_m(1+z)^3 + \Omega_\Lambda]$.
A 90% fraction means $\rho_m = 9\rho_\Lambda$.

quiz.prompt: Select all correct statements about the scaling of cosmic components.
quiz.solution: Photon number is conserved, so $n_\gamma\propto a^{-3}$; each photon's wavelength stretches, so its energy goes as $a^{-1}$, and the energy density scales as $a^{-4}$. A cosmological constant does not dilute. Matter–radiation equality ($z\approx 3400$) is much earlier than matter–Λ equality ($z\approx 0.3$).
hints: Combine the number density with the energy per photon to get the energy density.
choices: The photon number density scales as $a^{-3}$.
The energy of each photon scales as $a^{-1}$.
A cosmological constant has constant energy density as the universe expands.
The radiation energy density scales as $a^{-3}$ because the photon number density does.
Matter–radiation equality happens after matter–Λ equality.

mistakes: Treating the era boundaries as sharp. At $z_{\rm eq}$ matter and radiation contribute equally, and $a\propto t^{1/2}$ or $t^{2/3}$ is only approximate nearby.
Forgetting the neutrinos when computing the radiation density; they add about 69% to the photon density.
Using $\Omega_m$ where the physical density $\Omega_m h^2$ is needed, so that $h$ does not cancel.
Confusing matter–radiation equality ($z\approx 3400$) with matter–Λ equality ($z\approx 0.3$).

lessons.article:
The Friedmann equation says that the expansion rate is set by what is in the universe. Each component dilutes at its own rate, so the cosmic budget changes with time, and the universe passes through eras ruled by one component after another.

### The inventory

Densities scale as $\rho\propto a^{-3(1+w)}$ (week 3). The approximate present-day values below are standard fiducial numbers, to be checked against current data.

| component | $w$ | $\rho(a)$ | present value (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| photons (CMB) | $1/3$ | $a^{-4}$ | $\Omega_\gamma h^2 \approx 2.47\times10^{-5}$ |
| neutrinos | $1/3$ while relativistic | $a^{-4}$ early | $\Omega_\nu h^2 = \sum m_\nu/93.14\ \mathrm{eV}\gtrsim 6\times10^{-4}$ |
| baryons | $0$ | $a^{-3}$ | $\Omega_b h^2 \approx 0.0224$ |
| cold dark matter | $0$ | $a^{-3}$ | $\Omega_c h^2 \approx 0.120$ |
| curvature | $-1/3$ (effective) | $a^{-2}$ | $|\Omega_K|\lesssim 0.01$ |
| cosmological constant / dark energy | $-1$ | constant | $\Omega_\Lambda\approx 0.685$ |

With $h\approx 0.674$ this gives $\Omega_m\approx 0.315$ and $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.685$.

### Radiation density

A blackbody has energy density $\rho_\gamma c^2 = \dfrac{\pi^2}{15}\dfrac{(k_BT)^4}{(\hbar c)^3} = a_{\rm rad}T^4$ with $a_{\rm rad} = 7.566\times10^{-16}$ J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-4}$. For $T_0 = 2.7255$ K this gives $\Omega_\gamma h^2 \approx 2.47\times10^{-5}$.

The three neutrino species decouple before electron–positron annihilation and so are colder than the photons by $(4/11)^{1/3}$ (week 5). Treated as massless,
$$\rho_\nu = N_{\rm eff}\,\frac78\left(\frac{4}{11}\right)^{4/3}\rho_\gamma ,\qquad \Omega_r h^2 = \Omega_\gamma h^2\left[1 + 0.2271\,N_{\rm eff}\right]\approx 4.2\times10^{-5},$$
with $N_{\rm eff}\approx 3.046$. Massive neutrinos behave as radiation early and as matter later; we ignore that refinement here.

### The dimensionless expansion rate

Writing $H = H_0E(a)$,
$$E^2(a) = \Omega_r a^{-4} + \Omega_m a^{-3} + \Omega_K a^{-2} + \Omega_\Lambda .$$
Radiation dominates at small $a$, then matter, and (for the fiducial values) $\Lambda$ at late times. The transitions are gradual; "equality" means that the two densities are equal:
$$1+z_{\rm eq} = \frac{\Omega_m}{\Omega_r},\qquad 1+z_{m\Lambda} = \left(\frac{\Omega_\Lambda}{\Omega_m}\right)^{1/3}.$$
In the fiducial model $z_{\rm eq}\approx 3400$ and $z_{m\Lambda}\approx 0.30$.

### Matter and radiation eras: derivations

*Matter domination.* With $E^2 = \Omega_m a^{-3}$, $\dot a = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_m}\,a^{-1/2}$. Separate variables, $a^{1/2}da = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_m}\,dt$, and integrate from $a=0$:
$$a\propto t^{2/3},\qquad H = \frac{2}{3t},\qquad \rho_m = \frac{1}{6\pi G t^2}.$$

*Radiation domination.* With $E^2 = \Omega_r a^{-4}$, $\dot a = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r}\,a^{-1}$, so $a\,da = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r}\,dt$ and
$$a\propto t^{1/2},\qquad H = \frac{1}{2t},\qquad \rho_r = \frac{3}{32\pi G t^2}.$$
Since $\rho_r\propto T^4$, this gives $T\propto t^{-1/2}$, the heart of the thermal history in week 5.

*Dark-energy domination.* With $E^2 = \Omega_\Lambda$, $\dot a = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda}\,a$, which gives $a\propto e^{H_0\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda}\,t}$, de Sitter expansion.

These power laws are exact only for one component; near equality the full $E(a)$ must be integrated.

examples.title: Time and temperature
examples.problem: Using $H = 1.66\sqrt{g_*}\,T^2/M_{\rm Pl}$ with $M_{\rm Pl} = 1.221\times10^{19}$ GeV and $\hbar = 6.582\times10^{-25}$ GeV s, find the cosmic time at $T = 1$ MeV ($g_*=10.75$) and at $T = 100$ GeV ($g_* = 106.75$).
steps: In radiation domination $t = 1/(2H) = 1.12\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}}$. Multiply by $\hbar$ to convert: $t = 1.12\times10^{24}\times 6.582\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{s} = 0.74$ s.

Check the scaling: $t\propto g_*^{-1/2}T^{-2}$, so from 1 MeV to 100 GeV the time drops by $10^{-10}\times\sqrt{10.75/106.75}\approx 3\times10^{-11}$, consistent with $0.74\ \mathrm{s}\times 3.2\times10^{-11}$.

examples.title: The neutrino temperature today
examples.problem: Use entropy conservation to show that $T_\nu/T_\gamma = (4/11)^{1/3}$ after $e^\pm$ annihilation, and compute the neutrino temperature today for $T_0 = 2.7255$ K.
steps: After neutrinos decouple they free-stream, so $T_\nu\propto 1/a$ exactly. The photon–$e^\pm$ plasma conserves its own entropy: $g_{*s}\,(aT)^3$ is constant.
Before annihilation the plasma has $g_{*s} = 2 + \tfrac78\times4 = 11/2$ and temperature $T_{\rm before}$. After, only photons remain: $g_{*s}=2$.

Equating, $\tfrac{11}{2}(aT_{\rm before})^3 = 2(aT_\gamma)^3$, so $T_\gamma = (11/4)^{1/3}\,T_{\rm before}$. Neutrinos kept $T_\nu = T_{\rm before}$ (in the sense of the same $a$-scaling), so $T_\nu/T_\gamma = (4/11)^{1/3} = 0.714$.
Today $T_{\nu,0} = 0.714\times 2.7255\ \mathrm{K} = 1.945$ K, which corresponds to $k_BT_\nu\approx 1.7\times10^{-4}$ eV.

practice.prompt: The CMB temperature today is $T_0 = 2.7255$ K. Find $k_BT$ in eV at redshift $z = 1100$. Use $k_B = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K and give four significant figures.
hints: A blackbody cools as $T = T_0(1+z)$.

practice.prompt: At $T\sim 3$ MeV the relativistic species in equilibrium are photons ($g=2$), electrons and positrons ($g=4$ in total), and three neutrino species (each $\nu$ and $\bar\nu$ with one helicity, so $g=2$ per species). Find $g_*$.
hints: Bosons count fully and fermions count with a factor $7/8$.

practice.prompt: In radiation domination $t = 1/(2H)$ with $H = 1.66\sqrt{g_*}\,T^2/M_{\rm Pl}$. Take $g_* = 10.75$, $M_{\rm Pl} = 1.221\times10^{19}$ GeV and $\hbar = 6.582\times10^{-25}$ GeV s. Find the time in seconds when $T = 1$ MeV. Give three significant figures.
hints: Work in GeV: $T = 10^{-3}$ GeV. Compute $H$ in GeV first.
$t=1/(2H)$ is in GeV$^{-1}$; multiply by $\hbar$ in GeV s to get seconds.

practice.prompt: Why do weak interactions that keep neutrinos in equilibrium eventually "freeze out" as the universe cools?
practice.solution: In radiation domination $H\propto T^2$ while the weak rate scales roughly as $T^5$. Since $T^5$ falls faster, the ratio $\Gamma/H\propto T^3$ drops below 1 at $T\sim 1$ MeV.
hints: Compare how the two rates scale with $T$ in radiation domination.
choices: The interaction rate $\Gamma\propto T^5$ falls faster than the expansion rate $H\propto T^2$, so eventually $\Gamma<H$.
The universe stops expanding when it reaches $T\sim 1$ MeV.
The Hubble rate $H$ falls faster than the interaction rate, so $H$ becomes negligible.
Neutrinos become too massive to interact at low temperature.

practice.prompt: After $e^\pm$ annihilation the neutrinos have temperature $T_\nu = (4/11)^{1/3}T_\gamma$. Compute the effective degrees of freedom $(g_*,\ g_{*s})$ for photons plus three neutrino species (each with $g = 2$), giving three decimal places for each.
hints: Weight $g_*$ by $(T_\nu/T_\gamma)^4$ and $g_{*s}$ by $(T_\nu/T_\gamma)^3$.
The neutrino contribution is $\tfrac78\times 6\times(4/11)^{4/3}$ for $g_*$ and $\tfrac78\times6\times(4/11)$ for $g_{*s}$.

quiz.prompt: Model the neutrino interaction rate as $\Gamma = G_F^2T^5$ with $G_F = 1.166\times10^{-5}$ GeV$^{-2}$, and the expansion rate as $H = 1.66\sqrt{g_*}\,T^2/M_{\rm Pl}$ with $g_* = 10.75$ and $M_{\rm Pl} = 1.221\times10^{19}$ GeV. Find the temperature in MeV at which $\Gamma = H$. Give three significant figures.
quiz.solution: $T^3 = 1.66\times3.279/(1.360\times10^{-10}\times1.221\times10^{19}) = 3.28\times10^{-9}$ GeV$^3$, so $T = 1.486\times10^{-3}$ GeV $= 1.49$ MeV. This is an order-of-magnitude estimate; real decoupling is gradual.
hints: Divide both sides by $T^2$ to isolate $T^3$.
$T^3 = 1.66\sqrt{g_*}/(G_F^2M_{\rm Pl})$ in GeV$^3$; take the cube root and convert GeV to MeV.

quiz.prompt: At a temperature of about 5 MeV in the standard history, which species are relativistic and in thermal equilibrium?
quiz.solution: At 5 MeV photons, $e^\pm$ ($m_e = 0.511$ MeV) and neutrinos (still coupled, since decoupling is near 1 MeV) are relativistic and in equilibrium. Muons ($105.7$ MeV) have annihilated or decayed and are non-relativistic, and nucleons ($\sim 940$ MeV) are very non-relativistic with only a tiny abundance relative to photons.
hints: Compare each species' mass with $T\approx 5$ MeV, and recall when neutrinos decouple.
choices: Photons
Electrons and positrons
Neutrinos and antineutrinos
Muons and antimuons
Protons and neutrons

mistakes: Using $T\propto 1/a$ across an annihilation epoch without accounting for the change in $g_{*s}$.
Applying $t = 1/(2H)$ with a wrong $g_*$, or forgetting that the formula holds only during radiation domination.
Mixing units: in natural units $H$ comes out in GeV and must be converted to s$^{-1}$ with $\hbar$.

Counting a fermion's degrees of freedom without the factor $7/8$, or forgetting antiparticles and spin states (an $e^\pm$ pair gives $g=4$; each neutrino species gives $g=2$ for $\nu$ plus $\bar\nu$).

lessons.article:
The early universe was hot, dense and very nearly in thermal equilibrium, so a handful of numbers (a temperature and a list of species) determine its state. The cosmological questions then become: how fast does the temperature fall, and when do interactions become too slow to keep up?

### Conventions: natural units

In this lesson and the next, $\hbar = c = k_B = 1$. Temperatures are quoted as energies ($1\ \mathrm{MeV}\leftrightarrow 1.160\times10^{10}$ K), and times are converted using $\hbar = 6.582\times10^{-25}$ GeV s. The Planck mass here is $M_{\rm Pl} = G^{-1/2} = 1.221\times10^{19}$ GeV (the reduced Planck mass used for inflation in week 11 is smaller by $\sqrt{8\pi}$). Metric signature $(-,+,+,+)$ as before.

### Radiation and degrees of freedom

For relativistic species in equilibrium the energy and entropy densities are
$$\rho = \frac{\pi^2}{30}\,g_*\,T^4,\qquad s = \frac{2\pi^2}{45}\,g_{*s}\,T^3,$$
where each boson contributes its number of internal states $g$ and each fermion contributes $\tfrac78 g$. (If a species has its own temperature $T_i$, weight it by $(T_i/T)^4$ in $g_*$ and $(T_i/T)^3$ in $g_{*s}$.) Typical values:

- above about 200 GeV, every Standard Model particle counts: $g_* = 106.75$;
- at a few MeV: photons, $e^\pm$ and three neutrino species give $g_* = 2 + \tfrac78(4+6) = 10.75$;
- today: $g_* = 3.36$ and $g_{*s} = 3.91$.

### Time and temperature

Inserting $\rho$ into the Friedmann equation of week 3 for a flat universe gives
$$H = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi^3 g_*}{45}}\,\frac{T^2}{M_{\rm Pl}} \simeq 1.66\,\sqrt{g_*}\,\frac{T^2}{M_{\rm Pl}} .$$
In radiation domination $t = 1/(2H)$, which in convenient units is
$$t \approx \frac{2.42\ \mathrm{s}}{\sqrt{g_*}}\left(\frac{1\ \mathrm{MeV}}{T}\right)^{2}.$$
Conservation of entropy $s\,a^3$ means $T\propto g_{*s}^{-1/3}a^{-1}$, so $T\propto 1/a$ except when species annihilate and change $g_{*s}$. The estimate $t = 1/2H$ ignores changes in $g_*$ and is good to tens of percent across such transitions.

### Freeze-out

A reaction with rate $\Gamma$ per particle keeps a species in equilibrium while $\Gamma \gg H$. When $\Gamma$ falls below $H$, the average particle never meets another before the universe has expanded appreciably: the species **freezes out**. For weak interactions $\Gamma\sim G_F^2T^5$ falls much faster than $H\propto T^2$, so neutrinos decouple when $\Gamma\simeq H$, giving
$$T_{\rm dec}\sim\left(\frac{1.66\sqrt{g_*}}{G_F^2 M_{\rm Pl}}\right)^{1/3}\sim 1\ \mathrm{MeV}.$$

### Neutrinos are colder than photons

Shortly after neutrinos decouple, $e^\pm$ pairs annihilate (their abundance drops once $T\lesssim m_e = 0.511$ MeV) and dump their entropy into photons only. The plasma's entropy is conserved: $g_{*s}$ falls from $2 + \tfrac78\cdot 4 = 5.5$ to $2$, so $a T_\gamma$ rises by $(11/4)^{1/3}$ while $aT_\nu$ stays constant:
$$\frac{T_\nu}{T_\gamma} = \left(\frac{4}{11}\right)^{1/3} = 0.714,\qquad T_{\nu,0}\approx 1.945\ \mathrm{K}.$$

### A map of the early universe (approximate)

| event | temperature | time |
|---|---|---|
| electroweak crossover | $\sim 160$ GeV | $\sim 10^{-11}$ s |
| QCD crossover (quarks to hadrons) | $\sim 150$ MeV | $\sim 10^{-5}$ s |
| neutrino decoupling | $\sim 1$ MeV | $\sim 1$ s |
| $e^\pm$ annihilation | $\sim 0.5$ to $0.1$ MeV | $\sim 10$ s |
| nucleosynthesis | $\sim 0.1$ to $0.07$ MeV | $\sim 3$ min |
| matter–radiation equality | $\sim 0.8$ eV | $z\approx 3400$ |
| recombination | $\sim 0.26$ eV | $z\approx 1090$ |

Above the electroweak scale the particle content is a model assumption; below about 100 MeV the history is tied to laboratory physics.

examples.title: From freeze-out to the helium fraction
examples.problem: Take $T_f = 0.72$ MeV, $Q = 1.293$ MeV, $\tau_n = 880$ s, and let nucleosynthesis start after $180$ s. Estimate $Y_p$.
steps: Equilibrium ratio at freeze-out: $n/p = e^{-1.293/0.72} = e^{-1.796} = 0.166\approx 1/6$.
Neutron decay for 180 s multiplies the ratio by $e^{-180/880} = 0.815$, so $n/p = 0.166\times0.815 = 0.135$.
Nearly all neutrons go into ${}^4$He, so $Y_p = 2r/(1+r) = 0.270/1.135 = 0.238$.
The measured value is about 0.245. The estimate is within 3%, which is why $Y_p$ is such a robust test; the remaining difference comes from the gradual freeze-out and other small effects.

examples.title: Dating the nucleosynthesis epoch
examples.problem: Estimate the cosmic time at which $T = 0.08$ MeV using $T_0 = 2.7255$ K, $k_B = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K, $H_0 = 67.4$ km/s/Mpc and $\Omega_r = 9.2\times10^{-5}$.
steps: Present temperature in energy units: $k_BT_0 = 8.617\times10^{-5}\times 2.7255 = 2.349\times10^{-4}$ eV. Then $1+z = T/T_0 = 8\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{eV}/2.349\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} = 3.41\times10^{8}$, so $a = 2.94\times10^{-9}$.
The expansion rate is $H = 2.095\times10^{-20}\times(3.41\times10^8)^2 = 2.43\times10^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$.

Then $t = 1/(2H) \approx 206$ s, about 3.4 minutes, in agreement with the $g_*$ formula of week 5 ($2.42/\sqrt{3.36}\times(0.08)^{-2}\approx 206$ s) and with the "three minutes" quoted for nucleosynthesis.

practice.prompt: Using the equilibrium formula $n/p = e^{-Q/T}$ with $Q = 1.293$ MeV, find $n/p$ at $T = 1.0$ MeV. Give four significant figures.
hints: Substitute $T$ and $Q$ in the same units (MeV).

practice.prompt: At the start of nucleosynthesis there is one neutron for every 8 protons. If all neutrons are locked into ${}^4$He (two neutrons and two protons per nucleus), what is the helium mass fraction $Y_p$? Give three significant figures.
practice.solution: Take 1 neutron and 8 protons. They make $1/2$ of a ${}^4$He nucleus, which has mass number 4, so helium holds 2 nucleon masses out of 9. Then $Y_p = 2/9 = 0.222$.
hints: Count per neutron: how many ${}^4$He nuclei can it help build, and what fraction of all nucleons is that helium?
With $r = n/p$, $Y_p = 2r/(1+r)$.

practice.prompt: Free neutrons decay with mean lifetime $\tau_n = 880$ s. What fraction of the neutrons present survive for 300 s? Give three significant figures.
hints: Radioactive decay: $N(t) = N_0 e^{-t/\tau}$.

practice.prompt: Why does nucleosynthesis begin at $T\approx 0.07$ to $0.1$ MeV, even though the deuterium binding energy is $2.2$ MeV?
practice.solution: The photon distribution has a tail above $B_D$ even when $T\ll B_D$. Because there are so many photons per baryon, deuterium photodissociates until $\eta^{-1}e^{-B_D/T}\lesssim1$, which happens near $T\approx B_D/\ln(1/\eta)\approx 0.1$ MeV.
hints: Compare the number of photons in the tail above $B_D$ with the number of baryons.
choices: The neutrons have not yet frozen out at higher temperatures.
There are about $10^9$ photons per baryon, so photodissociation by the high-energy tail of the photon distribution destroys deuterium until $T$ is well below $B_D$.
Helium-4 cannot form until the universe is matter dominated.
Neutrinos are still in equilibrium and keep breaking up deuterium.

practice.prompt: Estimate the cosmic time at which the temperature is $T = 0.1$ MeV, treating the universe as radiation dominated with $H = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r}\,a^{-2}$ and $a = T_0/T$. Use $T_0 = 2.7255$ K, $k_B = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K, $H_0 = 67.4$ km/s/Mpc, $1\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 3.0857\times10^{19}$ km and $\Omega_r = 9.2\times10^{-5}$. Give the answer in seconds to three significant figures.
hints: Find $a$ from $T_0/T$ after converting both temperatures to eV.
Then $t = \int_0^a da'/(a'H) = a^2/(2H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r})$.

quiz.prompt: At freeze-out $n/p = 1/6$. Nucleosynthesis starts $240$ s later, and free neutrons decay with $\tau_n = 880$ s in the meantime. Estimate $Y_p = 2r/(1+r)$. Give three significant figures.
hints: First find $r = (1/6)e^{-t/\tau_n}$ at the start of nucleosynthesis.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following statements about standard nucleosynthesis are correct?
quiz.solution: More baryons per photon convert deuterium into helium more efficiently (D/H falls) and let deuterium survive at higher $T$. More relativistic species speed up expansion, freeze out $n/p$ earlier at a higher value, and raise $Y_p$. There are no stable $A=5$ or $A=8$ nuclei, so primordial carbon and oxygen are negligible.
hints: Think of how each change moves $T_f$, the photon-to-baryon ratio, and the bottleneck.
choices: Increasing the baryon-to-photon ratio $\eta$ decreases the predicted deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio.
Increasing $\eta$ makes the deuterium bottleneck break at a higher temperature, so nucleosynthesis starts earlier.
Additional relativistic species at the time of freeze-out raise the predicted $Y_p$.
The predicted $Y_p$ is independent of the number of relativistic species.
Stable nuclei with mass number 5 and 8 allow nucleosynthesis to produce abundant carbon and oxygen.

mistakes: Using $B_D = 2.2$ MeV as the temperature of nucleosynthesis; the huge photon-to-baryon ratio delays it to about 0.07 to 0.1 MeV.
Forgetting neutron decay between freeze-out and nucleosynthesis, or applying it for the wrong time.
Quoting $Y_p$ as a number fraction; here it is a mass fraction, $Y_p = 2r/(1+r)$.
Treating the lithium discrepancy as a "detection" of new physics; astrophysical and nuclear systematics are among the candidate explanations.

lessons.article:
Within the first few minutes the universe was a nuclear reactor with a fixed supply of fuel (protons and neutrons) and a very short operating time. A back-of-the-envelope estimate predicts that about a quarter of the baryonic mass ends up as helium-4, and that estimate is the main reason the hot big bang is taken seriously.

### Conventions

Natural units $\hbar=c=k_B=1$ as in week 5. Approximate inputs, to be checked against current data: neutron–proton mass difference $Q = m_n - m_p = 1.293$ MeV; neutron lifetime $\tau_n\approx 880$ s; deuterium binding energy $B_D = 2.224$ MeV; baryon-to-photon ratio $\eta = n_b/n_\gamma\approx 6.1\times10^{-10}$, equivalent to $\Omega_b h^2\approx 0.0224$.

### Neutron–proton balance

While weak reactions such as $n + \nu_e\leftrightarrow p + e^-$ are fast ($\Gamma>H$), the ratio of neutrons to protons follows its equilibrium value
$$\frac{n}{p} = e^{-Q/T}.$$
The rate falls faster than $H$ (week 5), so the ratio **freezes out** near $T_f\approx 0.7$ MeV with $n/p\approx 1/6$. After that only free neutron decay changes it:
$$\frac{n}{p}(t) = \left(\frac{n}{p}\right)_f e^{-t/\tau_n}.$$
By the start of nucleosynthesis, a few minutes later, $n/p\approx 1/7$.

### The deuterium bottleneck

Helium is built through deuterium, $n + p\leftrightarrow {\rm D} + \gamma$, but photons outnumber baryons by $1/\eta\approx 1.6\times10^9$. Even a tiny fraction of photons in the high-energy tail above $B_D$ is enough to destroy deuterium as fast as it forms. Deuterium survives only when
$$\frac{1}{\eta}\,e^{-B_D/T}\lesssim 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\lesssim \frac{B_D}{\ln(1/\eta)}\approx 0.1\ \mathrm{MeV},$$
and a careful calculation puts the onset near $T\approx 0.07$ to $0.08$ MeV, at about 3 minutes. This is far below $B_D$, so nucleosynthesis starts later and with fewer neutrons than a naive estimate based on $B_D$ would suggest.

### Helium and the trace elements

Once deuterium forms, essentially every available neutron ends up in ${}^4$He, the most tightly bound light nucleus. Because there is no stable nucleus with $A=5$ or $A=8$, the chain stops at traces of D, ${}^3$He and ${}^7$Li. Counting nucleons, with $n/p\equiv r$,
$$Y_p = \frac{2r}{1+r},$$
which gives $Y_p = 0.25$ for $r = 1/7$.

### Predictions and data

The standard calculation depends on $\eta$ and (weakly) on the number of relativistic species. Approximate observed values: $Y_p\approx 0.245$, ${\rm D/H}\approx 2.5\times10^{-5}$, ${}^7{\rm Li/H}\approx 1.6\times10^{-10}$. Deuterium and helium agree with the prediction for the same $\eta$ that the CMB infers independently; the predicted lithium is a factor of about 3 above the observed value (the **lithium problem**). Deuterium is the best "baryometer": its abundance falls steeply as $\eta$ increases. Extra relativistic species increase $H$ at a given $T$, freezing out $n/p$ earlier and at a higher value, and so raise $Y_p$; this constrains $N_{\rm eff}$.

### Estimating an epoch from temperature and expansion

To date an event, combine two scales. The temperature gives the scale factor, $a = T_0/T$ (valid while $g_{*s}$ is constant), and radiation domination gives $H = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r}\,a^{-2}$, so
$$t = \frac{1}{2H} = \frac{a^2}{2H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r}} .$$
This reproduces the $t\propto T^{-2}$ law of week 5 with the effective $g_*$ absorbed in $\Omega_r$. It is accurate to about one percent after $e^\pm$ annihilation ($T\lesssim0.1$ MeV). Before and during annihilation $g_*$ is larger and $T$ is not simply $T_0/a$, so it is off by up to a factor of about $2$: at $T=1$ MeV it gives $1.3$ s instead of $0.74$ s.

examples.title: The peak of the CMB spectrum
examples.problem:
Find the frequency of the maximum of $B_
u\propto
u^3/(e^{h
u/k_BT}-1)$ for $T = 2.7255$ K, using $k_B = 1.3806	imes10^{-23}$ J/K and $h = 6.626	imes10^{-34}$ J s.
steps: Let $x = h\nu/k_BT$. Setting $d/dx\,[x^3/(e^x-1)] = 0$ gives $3(e^x-1) = x\,e^x$, equivalently $x = 3(1 - e^{-x})$.
Iterate from $x=3$: $x\to 3(1-e^{-3}) = 2.851$, then $2.827$, then $2.8225$, converging to $x = 2.821$.

This is the peak of the spectrum per unit frequency; the peak per unit wavelength is at a different place ($\lambda_{\rm peak}T = 2.898\times10^{-3}$ m K, about 1.06 mm), because the two quantities are densities in different variables.

examples.title: Sound speed and acoustic scale
examples.problem: Take $\Omega_b h^2 = 0.0224$, $\Omega_\gamma h^2 = 2.47\times10^{-5}$, $z_* = 1090$, $r_s = 144.4$ Mpc and $D_M(z_*) = 13{,}870$ Mpc. Find $R$, $c_s/c$, $\theta_*$ and $\ell_A$.
steps: Sound speed: $c_s/c = 1/\sqrt{3(1+R)} = 1/\sqrt{3\times1.623} = 0.453$. The fluid is much stiffer than dust but slower than light by a factor of 2.2.
Acoustic scale: $\ell_A = \pi/\theta_* = 302$. The first peak at $\ell\approx 220$ is about $0.73\,\ell_A$ because of the phase shift.

practice.prompt: The CMB spectrum peaks at about $160.2$ GHz today. The peak frequency scales with temperature, $\nu\propto T\propto(1+z)$. Find the peak frequency, in THz, of the radiation at last scattering ($z=1090$). Give four significant figures.
practice.solution: $\nu = 160.2\ \mathrm{GHz}\times 1091 = 1.748\times10^{5}$ GHz $= 174.8$ THz, in the near infrared.
hints: The spectrum keeps its blackbody shape, so the peak frequency scales like the temperature.

practice.prompt: The solar system moves relative to the CMB rest frame at $v = 370$ km/s. Find the resulting dipole amplitude $\Delta T = T_0\,v/c$ in mK, for $T_0 = 2.7255$ K and $c = 299792$ km/s. Give three significant figures.
hints: To first order in $v/c$ the Doppler shift changes the temperature by $\Delta T/T = v/c$.

practice.prompt: Given $\Omega_b h^2 = 0.0224$ and $\Omega_\gamma h^2 = 2.47\times10^{-5}$, find the sound speed $c_s/c = 1/\sqrt{3(1+R)}$ of the photon–baryon fluid at $z = 1090$, where $R = \tfrac34\rho_b/\rho_\gamma$ and $\rho_b/\rho_\gamma$ scales as $a$. Give three significant figures.
hints: At $z=0$, $\rho_b/\rho_\gamma = \Omega_b/\Omega_\gamma = 0.0224/2.47\times10^{-5}$. Divide by $1+z$ to get its value at $z=1090$.

practice.prompt: What does the angular position of the acoustic peaks in the CMB power spectrum primarily measure?
practice.solution: The peaks mark the sound horizon, a standard ruler of comoving length $r_s$, as seen at the transverse comoving distance $D_M(z_*)$. Their spacing therefore gives $\theta_* = r_s/D_M$.
hints: A standard ruler of known physical size subtends an angle equal to its size divided by the appropriate distance.
choices: The ratio of the comoving sound horizon at last scattering to the transverse comoving distance to last scattering.
The age of the universe at last scattering.
The optical depth to reionization.
The Silk damping length alone.

practice.prompt: Use the Saha equation $\dfrac{x_e^2}{1-x_e} = \dfrac{1}{n_b}\left(\dfrac{m_ec^2\,k_BT}{2\pi(\hbar c)^2}\right)^{3/2}e^{-B/k_BT}$ with $n_b = \eta\,n_\gamma$ and $n_\gamma = \dfrac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}\left(\dfrac{k_BT}{\hbar c}\right)^3$, and take $\eta = 6.1\times10^{-10}$, $B = 13.6$ eV, $m_ec^2 = 510999$ eV, $\hbar c = 197.327$ eV nm, $\zeta(3) = 1.202$ and $k_B = 8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K. Find the temperature in K at which $x_e = 0.5$. Give three significant figures.
practice.solution: Setting the right side to $0.5$ and solving numerically gives $k_BT\approx 0.324$ eV, so $T\approx 3760$ K (a redshift near 1380). The actual last scattering is later because recombination is not in equilibrium.
hints: For $x_e = 1/2$ the left side equals $x_e^2/(1-x_e) = 0.25/0.5 = 0.5$.
Define $f(T)$ as right side minus $0.5$ and find its root numerically; the exponential makes it extremely steep, so bracket the root between 3000 K and 5000 K.

quiz.prompt: Compute the comoving sound horizon $r_s=\int_{z_*}^{\infty}c_s\,dz/H(z)$ at $z_*=1090$ in a flat universe with $\Omega_m=0.315$, $\Omega_r=9.2\times10^{-5}$ and $\Omega_\Lambda=1-\Omega_m-\Omega_r$, $H_0=67.4$ km/s/Mpc and $c=299792.458$ km/s. Use $c_s=c/\sqrt{3(1+R)}$ with $R=\tfrac34(0.0224/2.47\times10^{-5})/(1+z)$. Integrate up to $z=10^7$ (the contribution beyond is negligible). Give the answer in Mpc to three significant figures.
quiz.solution: Evaluating the integral numerically gives about $144$ Mpc, in line with the sound horizon at last scattering quoted in the article. The model is simplified (massless neutrinos, the simple form of $R$), so agreement at the percent level is expected.
hints: Write $H(z)=H_0\sqrt{\Omega_m(1+z)^3+\Omega_r(1+z)^4+\Omega_\Lambda}$.
The integrand varies over many decades in $1+z$; integrate numerically in $\ln(1+z)$ so that $dz=(1+z)\,d\ln(1+z)$.

quiz.prompt: Select all correct statements about the CMB.
quiz.solution: The statements about the blackbody spectrum, the dipole and the acoustic angular scale are correct. Recombination occurs near 0.3 eV because photons vastly outnumber baryons, and the peak position fixes only $\theta_*$, which depends on curvature, $H_0$ and $\Omega_m$ together.
hints: Consider which statements need extra assumptions or ignore the large photon-to-baryon ratio.
choices: Its spectrum is a blackbody to high precision, with temperature scaling as $T\propto(1+z)$.
The dipole is dominated by the motion of the solar system relative to the CMB rest frame.
The acoustic angular scale $\theta_*=r_s/D_M(z_*)$ constrains a combination of geometry and expansion history, not the Hubble constant alone.
Recombination occurs at $k_BT\approx 13.6$ eV, because that is the ionization energy of hydrogen.
The position of the first peak alone proves that the universe is spatially flat, whatever the other parameters.

mistakes: Assuming recombination happens at $k_BT\approx 13.6$ eV; the photon-to-baryon ratio pushes it down to about 0.3 eV.
Using the angular-diameter distance for a comoving ruler (use $D_M$ with a comoving $r_s$, or $d_A$ with a proper size).
Reading the first-peak position as a direct measurement of curvature; it constrains $\theta_*$, and curvature, $H_0$ and $\Omega_m$ are degenerate without other data.
Interpreting the dipole as primordial; it is dominated by our motion and is removed before the intrinsic anisotropy is analyzed.

lessons.article:
About 380,000 years after the big bang the universe became transparent. The photons that last scattered then are the CMB, a snapshot of the universe at $z\approx1090$, and they have travelled almost unimpeded ever since.

### Conventions and inputs

Approximate standard values, to be checked against current data: $T_0 = 2.7255$ K, last scattering at $z_*\approx 1090$ ($T_*\approx 2970$ K, $k_BT_*\approx 0.26$ eV), $\Omega_b h^2 \approx 0.0224$, $\Omega_\gamma h^2\approx 2.47\times10^{-5}$, comoving sound horizon $r_s\approx 144$ Mpc at last scattering, and comoving transverse distance $D_M(z_*)\approx 13.9$ Gpc. Signature $(-,+,+,+)$, flat geometry unless stated.

### From plasma to free streaming

Before recombination the gas is ionized and Thomson scattering ties photons to electrons, and through the Coulomb force to baryons. Recombination, $p + e^-\to {\rm H} + \gamma$, removes the free electrons. In equilibrium the ionization fraction $x_e$ follows the **Saha equation**
$$\frac{x_e^2}{1-x_e} = \frac{1}{n_b}\left(\frac{m_ek_BT}{2\pi\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}e^{-B/k_BT},\qquad n_b = \eta\,n_\gamma,\ \ B = 13.6\ \mathrm{eV}.$$
The same logic as the deuterium bottleneck applies: because photons outnumber baryons by $\sim10^9$, hydrogen stays ionized until $k_BT\approx 0.3$ eV, far below $B$. Saha gives $x_e = 1/2$ near 3760 K ($z\approx1380$). The real process is out of equilibrium (trapped Lyman-$\alpha$ photons and the slow two-photon $2s\to1s$ channel), so last scattering, defined as the peak of the visibility function where the optical depth reaches about 1, occurs later, at $z\approx1090$.

### A blackbody that stays a blackbody

The spectrum is $B_\nu\propto \nu^3/(e^{h\nu/k_BT}-1)$, peaking at $h\nu = 2.821\,k_BT$ (160 GHz today). Free streaming redshifts each photon by $1/(1+z)$ while conserving occupation numbers, so the spectrum remains a blackbody with $T\propto(1+z)$. Measured deviations from a blackbody are below $10^{-4}$ of the peak intensity.

### Anisotropies and the power spectrum

Expand the temperature field on the sky as $\Delta T/T(\hat n) = \sum a_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\hat n)$ and define $C_\ell = \langle|a_{\ell m}|^2\rangle$; an angular scale $\theta$ corresponds to $\ell\approx\pi/\theta$.

- **Dipole** ($\ell=1$): a Doppler effect from our motion, $\Delta T/T = v/c$. A speed near 370 km/s gives $\Delta T\approx 3.4$ mK, about a hundred times larger than the typical intrinsic anisotropy of order $10^{-5}T_0\approx 30\ \mu$K.
- **Large angles** ($\ell\lesssim 30$): the Sachs–Wolfe plateau, $\Delta T/T\approx\Phi/(3c^2)$ for the gravitational potential at last scattering.
- **Acoustic peaks**: before recombination gravity and radiation pressure drive standing sound waves in the photon–baryon fluid with sound speed
$$c_s = \frac{c}{\sqrt{3(1+R)}},\qquad R = \frac{3\rho_b}{4\rho_\gamma} \approx 0.62\ \text{at } z_*.$$
- **Silk damping** suppresses small scales, because photons diffuse out of small perturbations.
- **Polarization** arises from Thomson scattering of a local quadrupole; reionization at $z\sim 8$ (optical depth $\tau\approx0.054$) damps the anisotropy by $e^{-2\tau}$.

### The acoustic scale

The comoving sound horizon is $r_s = \int_{z_*}^\infty c_s\,dz/H(z)$. It is a standard ruler of angular size
$$\theta_* = \frac{r_s}{D_M(z_*)}\approx 0.0104\ \mathrm{rad},\qquad \ell_A \equiv\frac{\pi}{\theta_*}\approx 300 .$$
The first peak sits at $\ell\approx220$ rather than at $\ell_A$ because driving effects shift the oscillation phase, but the peak positions scale with $\ell_A$, so they measure the ratio of $r_s$ to $D_M$. That ratio constrains a combination of the expansion history and spatial curvature, not the curvature alone (the geometric degeneracy).

### What the peaks constrain

| feature | mainly constrains |
|---|---|
| peak positions | $\theta_*$, hence geometry and expansion history |
| odd to even peak height ratio | $\Omega_b h^2$ |
| overall peak heights | $\Omega_m h^2$ (matter–radiation equality) |
| tilt of the spectrum | $n_s$ |
| amplitude $\propto A_se^{-2\tau}$, low-$\ell$ polarization | $A_s$ and $\tau$ |

examples.title: Growing and decaying modes
examples.problem: Show that in a flat matter-only universe the solutions of $\ddot\delta + 2H\dot\delta = 4\pi G\bar\rho\,\delta$ are $\delta\propto t^{2/3}$ and $\delta\propto t^{-1}$.
steps: In the flat matter-only universe $a\propto t^{2/3}$, so $H = 2/(3t)$. The Friedmann equation gives $4\pi G\bar\rho = \tfrac32H^2 = \tfrac32\cdot\tfrac{4}{9t^2} = \tfrac{2}{3t^2}$.
Substitute $\delta = t^p$: $\ddot\delta = p(p-1)t^{p-2}$ and $2H\dot\delta = \tfrac43 p\,t^{p-2}$. The equation becomes $p(p-1) + \tfrac43p = \tfrac23$.
Rearrange to $p^2 + \tfrac13p - \tfrac23 = 0$, equivalently $3p^2 + p - 2 = 0$, which factorizes as $(3p-2)(p+1)=0$.
Therefore $p = 2/3$ (growing, $\propto a$) or $p = -1$ (decaying, $\propto a^{-3/2}$). Only the growing mode matters after a few expansion times.

examples.title: How much can linear growth do?
examples.problem: A baryon density perturbation has $\delta = 10^{-5}$ at recombination ($z=1100$). Estimate its linear value today if it grows like $D(a)$ with $D(1)=0.78$ and $D\simeq a$ at $z=1100$.
steps: The growth factor is $D(1)/D(a_*) = 0.78\times1101 = 859$.
Therefore $\delta_0 = 10^{-5}\times 859 \approx 0.009$.

This is far below $\delta\sim1$, the scale at which structure becomes nonlinear. Hence the argument for collisionless dark matter, which can start growing before recombination. The argument is simplified, since baryon perturbations also oscillate acoustically before recombination.

practice.prompt: In a flat matter-dominated universe the growing mode is $\delta\propto a$. By what factor does a linear perturbation grow between $z=9$ and $z=0$?

Seek power-law solutions $\delta\propto t^p$ of $\ddot\delta + 2H\dot\delta = 4\pi G\bar\rho\,\delta$ in a flat matter-only universe, where $H = 2/(3t)$ and $4\pi G\bar\rho = 2/(3t^2)$. List both exponents $p$.
hints: Substitute $\delta=t^p$ and divide by $t^{p-2}$ to get an algebraic equation for $p$.
The equation is quadratic: $p(p-1) + \tfrac43p - \tfrac23 = 0$.

practice.prompt: Which equation governs the linear growth of the density contrast $\delta$ of pressureless matter on sub-horizon scales in an expanding universe?
practice.solution: The gravitational source term has the sign that drives growth, and the $2H\dot\delta$ term is the friction from expansion. The wrong-sign version would oscillate, and removing the friction (as in a static, non-expanding medium) would give exponential rather than power-law growth.
hints: Gravity should amplify an overdensity, and expansion should act as friction.
choices: $\ddot\delta + 2H\dot\delta - 4\pi G\bar\rho\,\delta = 0$
$\ddot\delta + 2H\dot\delta + 4\pi G\bar\rho\,\delta = 0$
$\ddot\delta + 4\pi G\bar\rho\,\delta = 0$
$\dot\delta = 4\pi G\bar\rho\,\delta$

practice.prompt: Estimate the equality wavenumber $k_{\rm eq} = a_{\rm eq}H_{\rm eq}/c$ for a flat universe with $\Omega_m = 0.315$, $H_0 = 67.4$ km/s/Mpc and $1+z_{\rm eq}=3401$, where radiation density equals matter density (so $\Omega_r = \Omega_m/3401$ and $H = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_m(1+z)^3 + \Omega_r(1+z)^4}$ at equality). Use $c=299792.458$ km/s and give the answer in Mpc$^{-1}$ to three significant figures.
hints: At equality the two terms under the square root are equal, so $H_{\rm eq} = H_0\sqrt{2\Omega_m}\,(1+z_{\rm eq})^{3/2}$.

practice.prompt: A colleague argues: "The CMB temperature fluctuations are about $10^{-5}$, so the universe is clearly not homogeneous and the Friedmann equations cannot apply." Respond using the distinction between background and perturbation: say what is homogeneous, what is not, which equations govern each, and when linear theory stops being valid.
practice.solution: The background quantities $a(t)$, $H(t)$, $\bar\rho(t)$ and $\bar T(t)$ are the spatial averages and depend only on time; they obey the Friedmann equations. The inhomogeneity is carried by small perturbations $\delta(\mathbf x,t)$, $\Phi(\mathbf x,t)$ and $\delta T(\mathbf x,t)$ with $|\delta|\sim10^{-5}\ll1$, which obey equations linearized about the background. Homogeneity is a statement about the statistics of the perturbations and the background, not about every point being identical. At recombination the perturbations are tiny, so the background description is excellent. As $\delta$ grows and approaches 1 (galaxies and clusters today), linear theory fails and nonlinear methods such as N-body simulations are needed, while the average expansion is still governed by the Friedmann equations.
hints: Ask which quantity depends only on $t$ and which depends on $\mathbf x$ as well, and compare the size of $\delta$ with 1.
rubric: Identifies the background ($a$, $H$, $\bar\rho$, $\bar T$) as functions of time only and the Friedmann equations as their equations.
Identifies the perturbations ($\delta$, $\Phi$, $\delta T$) as small deviations obeying linearized equations.
States that linear theory requires $|\delta|\ll1$ and fails for galaxies and clusters today, without invalidating the background.

quiz.prompt: For a flat universe with $\Omega_m=0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda=0.7$, the growth factor is $D(a)=\tfrac52\Omega_m H(a)/H_0\int_0^a da'/[a'H(a')/H_0]^3$ with $H(a)/H_0 = \sqrt{0.3a^{-3}+0.7}$. Find the ratio $D(z=1)/D(z=0)$, to three significant figures.
quiz.solution: Numerically $D(1)=0.779$ and $D(0.5)=0.477$, so $D(z=1)/D(z=0) = 0.612$. In a matter-only universe the ratio would be $0.5$; the cosmological constant suppresses late-time growth, so the ratio is larger.
hints: Evaluate $D$ at $a=0.5$ and $a=1$ with the same normalization.

quiz.prompt: Select all quantities that belong to the homogeneous background rather than to the perturbations.
quiz.solution: $a(t)$, $\bar\rho(t)$ and $H(t)$ depend on time only and obey the Friedmann equations. The density contrast $\delta$ and the potential perturbation $\Phi$ depend on position and are perturbations governed by linearized equations.
hints: Background quantities depend on time only.
choices: The scale factor $a(t)$
The mean matter density $\bar\rho(t)$
The Hubble parameter $H(t)$
The density contrast $\delta(\mathbf x,t)$
The gravitational potential perturbation $\Phi(\mathbf x,t)$

mistakes: Mixing up comoving and proper wavenumbers, or applying the sub-horizon (Newtonian) equation to super-horizon modes.
Continuing to use linear theory when $\delta\sim1$; linear extrapolation tells you where structure becomes nonlinear, not what happens after.
Forgetting the Hubble friction term $2H\dot\delta$. Without it the growth is far too fast: exponential in a static medium, and $t^{1.46}$ instead of $t^{2/3}$ in a matter-dominated universe.
Treating $\delta T/T\sim10^{-5}$ as a failure of homogeneity; homogeneity describes the background, and perturbations are small deviations.

Compute growth factors and the equality scale k_eq, and explain the shape of the matter power spectrum.

lessons.article:
Everything so far described the smooth universe. Real structure is a small departure from smoothness, and the method is to split every field into a background that depends only on time and a perturbation that depends on position as well.

### Background versus perturbation

Write $\rho(\mathbf x, t) = \bar\rho(t)\,[1 + \delta(\mathbf x, t)]$ and likewise for the potential, velocities and temperature. The **background** ($a(t)$, $H(t)$, $\bar\rho(t)$, $\bar T(t)$) obeys the Friedmann equations. The **perturbations** ($\delta$, $\Phi$, $\delta T$) obey equations obtained by expanding Einstein's equations to first order in small quantities; this is **linear theory**, valid while $|\delta|\ll1$. The CMB has $\delta T/T\sim10^{-5}$, safely linear; galaxies today have $\delta\gg1$ and need nonlinear methods.

### Conventions

Comoving coordinate $\mathbf x$ so that proper position is $a\mathbf x$; $\nabla$ is the comoving gradient; $H = \dot a/a$; peculiar velocity $\mathbf v$; metric signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Fiducial values (approximate, check against current data): $\Omega_m\approx0.315$, $\Omega_\Lambda\approx0.685$, $H_0\approx67.4$ km/s/Mpc, $n_s\approx0.965$, $\sigma_8\approx 0.81$.

### The growth equation

For pressureless matter on scales well inside the horizon, Newtonian physics in comoving coordinates suffices:
$$\dot\delta + \frac1a\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf v = 0,\qquad \dot{\mathbf v} + H\mathbf v = -\frac1a\nabla\Phi,\qquad \nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\bar\rho\,a^2\delta .$$
Eliminating $\mathbf v$ and $\Phi$ gives
$$\ddot\delta + 2H\dot\delta = 4\pi G\bar\rho\,\delta .$$
The right side is gravity pulling overdensities together; the term $2H\dot\delta$ is Hubble friction, which slows growth. The equation has no $k$-dependence, so every Fourier mode $\delta_k$ grows by the same factor.

### Solutions

In a matter-dominated flat universe $H = 2/(3t)$ and $4\pi G\bar\rho = \tfrac32H^2 = 2/(3t^2)$. Try $\delta\propto t^p$:
$$p(p-1) + \tfrac43 p = \tfrac23\ \Longrightarrow\ p = \tfrac23\ \text{or}\ p = -1 .$$
The **growing mode** is $\delta_+\propto t^{2/3}\propto a$ and the **decaying mode** is $\delta_-\propto t^{-1}\propto a^{-3/2}$. During radiation domination, sub-horizon dark-matter perturbations grow only logarithmically because $H$ is set by the radiation (the Mészáros effect). With a cosmological constant, growth slows at late times. The solution is $\delta\propto D(a)$ with
$$D(a) = \frac52\,\Omega_m H_0^2\,H(a)\int_0^a\frac{da'}{[a'H(a')]^3},$$
normalized so that $D\to a$ early on. For $\Omega_m=0.3$, $\Omega_\Lambda=0.7$, $D(1)\approx0.78$. The growth rate $f\equiv d\ln D/d\ln a$ is well approximated by $\Omega_m(a)^{0.55}$ in $\Lambda$CDM.

### Horizon scales and the power spectrum

The comoving Hubble radius is $c/(aH)$. A mode with comoving wavenumber $k$ is super-horizon for $k\ll aH/c$ and enters the horizon when $k = aH/c$. Modes that enter during the radiation era have their growth suppressed, so the matter power spectrum $P(k)\propto k^{n_s}T^2(k)$ turns over near the horizon scale at equality,
$$k_{\rm eq} = \frac{a_{\rm eq}H_{\rm eq}}{c}\approx 0.01\ \mathrm{Mpc^{-1}},$$
rising as $k^{n_s}$ at lower $k$ and falling roughly as $k^{n_s-4}$, with logarithmic corrections, at higher $k$. The turnover position depends on $\Omega_m h^2$, which is how large-scale structure measures matter density.

### Why baryons alone are not enough

Before recombination baryons are coupled to photons and cannot collapse. Afterwards a perturbation of size $\sim10^{-5}$ grows like $D(a)$, about a factor of $860$ in $\Lambda$CDM, to $\delta\sim0.01$ today, far short of the $\delta\gg1$ seen in galaxies. Collisionless dark matter, which does not feel the photons, starts growing earlier. This is a qualitative argument; a full numerical calculation, beyond this course, makes it quantitative.

examples.title: Mass from a flat rotation curve
examples.problem: A spiral galaxy has a flat circular speed $v_c = 200$ km/s out to $r = 20$ kpc. Estimate the enclosed mass in solar masses, and the mass enclosed at $40$ kpc if the curve stays flat.
steps: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: $v_c^2/r = GM/r^2$, so $M(<r) = v_c^2r/G$.
Convert: $v_c = 2.0\times10^{5}$ m/s and $r = 20\times3.0857\times10^{19} = 6.171\times10^{20}$ m.

A flat curve means $M(<r)\propto r$, so at $40$ kpc the enclosed mass doubles to about $3.7\times10^{11}M_\odot$. The stars and gas of such a galaxy total a few $\times10^{10}M_\odot$, so most of the enclosed mass is not visible.

u = 0.06$ eV and $\Omega_m h^2 = 0.1424$. Find $\Omega_

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are lines of evidence for dark matter that do not depend on a specific particle model?
quiz.solution: Rotation curves, lensing masses and the CMB all show the gravitational effects of non-baryonic matter. No laboratory detection has been confirmed, and nucleosynthesis constrains the baryon density but says nothing about weakly interacting massive particles.
hints: Evidence of this kind is gravitational or cosmological; none of it measures the particle's properties.
choices: Flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies.
Cluster masses from lensing that exceed the baryonic mass.
CMB acoustic peak heights that require $\Omega_m h^2$ well above $\Omega_b h^2$.
A confirmed laboratory detection of a dark matter particle.
Light-element abundances showing that the dark matter is a weakly interacting massive particle.

Using visible light as a tracer of mass in clusters and lensing, instead of the dynamics or the shear.
Confusing the neutrino mass sum with the mass of one species, or forgetting that cosmological limits are model dependent.
Assuming the NFW profile is exact; it is a fit with scatter, and its inner slope is an open comparison with observations.
